data.regions: Nigeria ‐ with a focus on Bauchi State and communities in Northern Nigeria
data.additional: REDYWEI is particularly interested in contributing to discussions that connect mental health with community resilience, youth empowerment, disability inclusion, and access to psychosocial support. We would welcome opportunities to collaborate with PAMHO beyond the Conversation, including knowledge-sharing, community engagement, and future initiatives that strengthen mental health awareness and support at community level.
data.description:
Resilient Development for Youths and Women Empowerment Initiative (REDYWEI) is a Nigerian community-focused organization working to promote resilience, empowerment, participation, and sustainable development among young people, women, and underserved communities.

Our work includes youth and women empowerment, community engagement, health awareness, resilience building, and initiatives that respond to social and community challenges. Through our programmes and community activities, REDYWEI has increasingly focused on mental health and emotional wellbeing, disability inclusion, and creating safe spaces where people can openly discuss issues affecting their lives and wellbeing.

REDYWEI uses community-based dialogue, awareness activities, capacity building, partnerships, and participatory approaches that place community voices and lived experiences at the centre of our work. We also use creative methods such as Cellphilms and Photovoice to enable young people and underserved communities to express and document their experiences and perspectives.

We believe that sustainable development is strengthened when communities are empowered, included, heard, and supported to build resilience and participate in solutions that affect their lives. Our growing work in mental health and emotional wellbeing reflects this commitment to people-centred community development.
data.contribution:
REDYWEI would contribute to the Pan-African Mental Health Conversation by using our community networks, digital platforms, and grassroots experience to amplify the conversation and encourage meaningful participation from young people, women, persons with disabilities, and underserved communities.

We can support the mobilization of community members and relevant stakeholders, promote the Conversation through our social media and networks, and share community perspectives on mental health, emotional wellbeing, resilience, psychosocial support, disability inclusion, and stigma reduction.

As part of our community engagement approach, REDYWEI uses participatory visual methods, including Cellphilms and Photovoice, to enable young people and underserved communities to document and communicate their lived experiences. We believe these approaches can help bring authentic grassroots voices into continental mental health discussions.

We would also be interested in supporting awareness campaigns, content amplification, community engagement, knowledge-sharing, and future collaborative initiatives with PAMHO.

Through this partnership, REDYWEI hopes not only to contribute our grassroots experience but also to learn from other African organizations, build meaningful institutional relationships, and strengthen collective efforts toward a more inclusive, accessible, and people-centred mental health agenda across Africa.

data.why:
I want to become a Pan-African Mental Health Conversation Ambassador because I have come to recognise how deeply mental health is still under-prioritised across our communities. While awareness is growing, significant gaps remain around stigma, misinformation, fear and access to support.

Last year, I founded a mental health NGO focused on creating safe, open and relatable conversations around mental health. Through this work, I hope to take mental health awareness and intervention closer to communities, making support as free and accessible as possible.

Becoming an Ambassador would strengthen my ability to contribute to this vision by expanding my knowledge, network, reach and access to resources and partnerships across Africa. I would also bring these opportunities back to ADVORE, helping us develop stronger programmes and reach more people. Ultimately, I want to contribute to a culture where mental health is everyone’s business and is valued as seriously as physical health.
data.meaning:
To me, mental health is more than the absence of mental illness; it is something that can save a person’s life, support someone’s success, and contribute to healthier communities. It affects how we think, feel, relate to others, respond to challenges, and participate in society.

For Africa, mental health matters because the wellbeing of our people is connected to the wellbeing and development of our communities and continent. When people understand their mental health, can seek support without shame, and have access to appropriate care, they are better able to learn, work, build relationships, and contribute meaningfully to society.

I believe mental health should be accessible to everyone, regardless of income or location. We need to make mental health information, conversations, and support as free and accessible as possible.

Ultimately, investing in mental health is investing in Africa. Healthier individuals and communities can foster the empathy, understanding, connection, and collective strength needed to build a stronger Africa, not only within individual countries, but as Africans connected by a shared commitment to wellbeing, dignity, progress, and unity across our diverse communities.
data.promote:
I will promote the mental health conversation by using both my existing network and the platforms I am building through ADVORE to make mental health discussions more open, relatable and accessible.

Through ADVORE, I will organise conversations, awareness activities, community outreaches, webinars and interactive sessions that encourage people to speak about mental health without fear or judgement. I will also use social media platforms such as Instagram, TikTok, WhatsApp and LinkedIn to share educational, relatable and engaging content that challenges stigma, corrects misinformation and encourages people to recognise when they may need support.

I will actively engage young people, schools, universities, community groups and other organisations, creating opportunities for mental health professionals and people with lived experiences to share their perspectives.

As a Pan-African Mental Health Conversation Ambassador, I would also use the knowledge, resources and networks gained to strengthen ADVORE’s programmes and extend our reach. My goal is to make mental health conversations a normal part of everyday community life and encourage people to see seeking help as a strength, not a weakness.
data.priorDetails:
Through ADVORE, I have been involved in several initiatives that promote mental health awareness, open conversations and safe spaces. We partnered on a Boy and Girl Child Conference where students were given a safe and supportive environment to share their thoughts and discuss struggles they may be experiencing.

We organised a Men’s Check-In Café focused on men’s mental health, creating an informal space for men to have honest conversations about their wellbeing. We also delivered an autism awareness session in a school in Abuja, highlighting the importance of neurotypical communities understanding and supporting neurodivergent people as part of creating more inclusive environments.

We created a safe space for cancer survivors, providing short-term therapy alongside wellness activities. We are currently developing a school mental health programme that will take awareness sessions on relevant mental health topics to students.

In addition, ADVORE consistently hosts virtual fireside chats on mental health-related issues, helping remove geographical and accessibility barriers so that people can participate from anywhere.

data.why:
I want to become a Pan-African Mental Health Conversation Ambassador because I believe mental health is fundamental to health, dignity, resilience, and sustainable community development across Africa. With over nine years of experience as a mental health and psychosocial support practitioner, I have witnessed how stigma, trauma, displacement, limited resources, and inadequate services prevent individuals and communities from accessing the support they need to heal and thrive.

My professional journey has deepened my commitment to creating safe, inclusive, and culturally responsive spaces where mental health can be discussed openly and without judgement. I hold a Bachelor of Arts in Psychology and a Postgraduate Certificate in Perinatal Mental Health, and I am currently pursuing a Master’s degree in Organizational Psychology.

Transitioning from Namibia to Zambia has broadened my understanding of the mental health challenges facing underserved communities and strengthened my belief in locally led, practical, and sustainable solutions. In Zambia, I am contributing to stronger community mental health systems through trauma-informed care, capacity building for frontline workers, referral networks, and accessible psychological and psychosocial support.

As an Ambassador, I want to use my experience, voice, and passion to amplify mental health conversations, challenge stigma, promote early help-seeking, and strengthen collaboration across African communities and systems. I see this opportunity as a platform to learn from diverse African perspectives while sharing practical experiences from my own work.

Ultimately, I want to contribute to a Pan-African movement where mental health is prioritized, conversations are normalized, and every individual and community has the opportunity to access support, build resilience, and thrive.
data.meaning:
To me, mental health means having the emotional, psychological, and social wellbeing to navigate life, heal from adversity, build resilience, and experience a sense of belonging and hope. It is not simply the absence of mental illness; it is about creating environments where individuals and communities feel safe, supported, heard, and empowered to thrive.

My understanding of mental health has also been shaped by my own healing journey. Going through my own experiences made me realize how important it is to create more open conversations about mental health and, equally, to ensure that people can access appropriate support when they need it. Healing should not be a journey people have to navigate alone.

Mental health matters for Africa because our communities continue to experience the effects of poverty, trauma, displacement, violence, health crises, unemployment, and other social and economic pressures. Yet stigma, limited resources, and inadequate access to services often prevent people from seeking help. Investing in mental health is therefore an investment in healthier families, stronger communities, productive workplaces, and Africa’s future.

I am currently based in Kabwe, Zambia, where I am working with a team  of Psychosocial ,counselors , community caregivers and psychologist   towards establishing Kabwe’s first Trauma and Resilience Centre. My vision is to create a safe, accessible, community-based space where people can receive psychosocial support, develop resilience, and begin their healing journey. Through this work, I hope to turn mental health conversations into meaningful, accessible action.
data.promote:
I will promote mental health conversations by leveraging my professional networks, community relationships, and digital platforms across Namibia and Zambia. Over the past nine years, I have built meaningful connections with mental health and psychosocial support practitioners, community organizations, frontline workers, and other stakeholders committed to improving mental health outcomes. I see these networks as an important foundation for strengthening cross-border learning, collaboration, referrals, and collective action.

In Zambia, I will continue creating safe spaces for dialogue within communities, encouraging open conversations about mental health, trauma, resilience, and psychosocial wellbeing. I will also engage frontline workers and community leaders to help bring mental health conversations closer to the people who need them most.

I am already actively engaged in social mobility and community engagement through Facebook, where I have a growing network of more than 5,000 followers. I will use this platform to share accessible mental health information, challenge stigma, promote help-seeking, highlight local resources, and amplify African voices and lived experiences.

My networks in Namibia and Zambia will also provide opportunities to connect practitioners, organizations, and communities through knowledge-sharing and collaborative initiatives.
data.priorDetails:
My mental health advocacy and related work spans has a strong focus on psychosocial support, trauma-informed care, community engagement, capacity building, and mental health awareness.

In Namibia, I worked with Childline Lifeline, providing psychosocial support and counselling to children, young people, and families experiencing emotional and social challenges. I also supported the Office of the First Lady of Namibia, where I provided trauma-informed care and counselling during the COVID-19 pandemic. This work highlighted the importance of accessible psychological support during times of crisis and strengthened my commitment to advocating for mental health services within communities.

I was also involved in mental health advocacy initiatives supporting refugees in Osire Refugee Camp (Namibia), where I contributed to efforts aimed at addressing trauma, psychosocial wellbeing, and access to support among displaced populations. These experiences reinforced my belief that mental health services must be culturally responsive, community-based, and accessible to vulnerable populations.

Beyond direct service delivery, I served as a co-host of a mental health radio program on the Namibian Broadcasting Network, using media to create public conversations, increase awareness, challenge stigma, and encourage help-seeking.

I have also contributed to professional capacity building by tutoring at the Namibia University of Science and Technology and developing a Care and Counselling Manual to support  students in providing effective psychosocial care.

data.description:
SheHealed Health & Advocacy Initiatives is a women- and girl-focused organization dedicated to promoting health, emotional healing, and empowerment. We advocate for women and girls to live healthy, informed, and dignified lives, while creating safe spaces where they can be heard, supported, and encouraged to thrive.
Our work focuses on women’s health, mental health advocacy, menstrual health education, girl-child empowerment, and community outreach. Through awareness campaigns, educational programs, skills acquisition, and partnerships, we address challenges that affect women and girls, including limited access to health information, menstrual hygiene challenges, emotional distress, and barriers to personal development.
We believe that every woman and girl deserves access to accurate health information, emotional support, and opportunities to reach her full potential. Our approach combines education, advocacy, compassion, and practical community action to create meaningful and lasting change.
SheHealed is committed to building a healthier, more empowered generation of women and girls, one conversation, one intervention, and one community at a time. We welcome individuals, organizations, and partners who share our vision of a world where women and girls are supported, respected, and empowered to thrive.

We will contribute by sharing practical insights from our work with communities, particularly on the emotional and social challenges affecting women and girls. Through awareness campaigns, educational sessions, and advocacy activities, we will help promote early recognition of mental health concerns, encourage supportive conversations, and strengthen knowledge of available help.

Our experience coordinating volunteers and implementing health-focused initiatives can help translate shared mental health goals into practical activities at the grassroots level.

Beyond our local work, SheHealed will contribute to cross-country learning by sharing experiences, challenges, and lessons from our advocacy activities. We are committed to learning from other African organizations and adapting effective approaches to our own communities.

Through collaboration, we hope to strengthen mental health advocacy, amplify the voices of women and girls, and contribute to a more informed, compassionate, and supportive Africa where mental health is treated as an essential part of overall well-being.

data.meaning:
To me, mental health means having a healthy emotional, psychological, and social well-being that enables a person to cope with life’s challenges, build meaningful relationships, make sound decisions, and live with purpose. It is not simply the absence of mental illness; it is about creating an environment where people can openly discuss their struggles and receive support without shame or discrimination.

Mental health matters greatly for Africa because many people face challenges such as unemployment, poverty, insecurity, social pressure, displacement, and limited access to quality healthcare. Yet mental health is often overlooked because of stigma, cultural misconceptions, and a lack of awareness and affordable services.

Promoting mental health can help young people, families, workplaces, and communities become more resilient and productive. Africa needs to normalize conversations about mental health, encourage early support, strengthen community-based services, and empower people to seek help without fear of judgment.

I believe that a mentally healthy Africa is one where people are heard, supported, valued, and given the opportunity to thrive.

My responsibilities included facilitating psychoeducation sessions, participating in group discussions, supporting clients through therapeutic activities, and working alongside a multidisciplinary team that included counsellors, nurses, psychiatrists, and other professionals. The platform allowed us to engage listeners in meaningful discussions and promote help-seeking behaviour.I have also participated in youth and mental health forums, symposiums, and advocacy initiatives, while using social media to promote awareness and encourage open conversations about mental health. These experiences have strengthened my commitment to mental health advocacy and my desire to contribute to improved mental health outcomes across Africa.

data.meaning:
To me, mental health is the foundation of a person's overall well-being. It influences how we think, feel, cope with challenges, build relationships, and contribute to our communities. Good mental health is not simply the absence of mental illness; it is the ability to lead a balanced, productive, and fulfilling life despite life's challenges.

These challenges can significantly affect people's emotional and psychological well-being. By prioritizing mental health, Africa can unlock the full potential of its people. Promoting mental health awareness also helps create more compassionate and resilient communities where people feel safe to speak openly about their struggles and seek help without fear of judgment.

data.meaning:
Every day, I navigate life as an American residing in Ghana, stepping into a vibrant West African reality vastly different from where I grew up. Yet, bridging these two worlds has revealed one universal truth: our minds require the same tender care, no matter which side of the Atlantic we call home.

In the United States, mental health discussions are highly visible but often deeply isolating. Conversely, in Ghana, I have experienced the beautiful warmth of communal living, alongside a heavy, traditional silence around emotional suffering, in which I have witnessed it being dismissed as a Western concept or a spiritual failing.

But mental wellness is a universal human right, not a cultural luxury. Africa possesses the youngest, most dynamic population in the world, but our youth cannot innovate or lead if they are forced to carry trauma, anxiety, and depression in secret. My goal as an ambassador is not to import Western fixes, but to help decolonize well-being. I want to champion a holistic African tradition where mind, body, and spirit work together.

By serving as a Pan-African Mental Health Conversation Ambassador, I will leverage my unique transnational network to build safe spaces, dismantle taboos, and heal our global community together.
